identification.summary: China-based cyber-espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Hexagon Typhoon and maps to APT12, Numbered Panda, Calc Team, DNS-Calc, HYDROGEN, Red Anubis and HORDE [S1]. MITRE ATT&CK describes APT12 as a group attributed to China that has targeted media outlets, high-tech companies and multiple governments [S4]. Mandiant reported that APT12 compromised the New York Times in October 2012 and that in 2014 it ran spear-phishing campaigns against organizations in Taiwan and Japan [S2]. Mandiant also documented a repeated pattern: after public exposure, the group paused briefly and then retooled [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Ixeshe malware, which MITRE associates with APT12, has been used since at least 2009 against targets in East Asia [S4][S7]. Arbor Networks (as reported by Mandiant) dated RIPTIDE campaigns to March 2011 [S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Hexagon Typhoon. Microsoft lists HYDROGEN, NUMBERED PANDA, Calc Team, Red Anubis, APT12, DNS-Calc and HORDE as other names [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as APT12 (G0005) with associated names IXESHE, DynCalc, Numbered Panda and DNSCALC [S4]. Mandiant uses APT12 and lists 'Calc Team' as an alias [S3]. MISP Galaxy lists BRONZE GLOBE (Secureworks), BeeBus, Group 22 and Crimson Iron as synonyms [S8]. Do not confuse this actor with APT5 / Mulberry Typhoon (MANGANESE). The imported summary text in this record described APT5 and has been replaced.

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China. Mandiant says APT12 is 'believed to be a cyber espionage group thought to have links to the Chinese People's Liberation Army' [S2][S3]. MITRE records the group as attributed to China [S4], and Microsoft lists its origin as China [S1].
attribution.confidence: Mandiant's PLA link is hedged ('believed to be', 'thought to have links') and does not name a specific unit [S2][S3]. MISP Galaxy, citing CFR data, records China as the suspected state sponsor with an attribution-confidence value of 50 [S8]. No government indictment or formal government attribution naming APT12 was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Vendor technical reporting from Mandiant/FireEye on malware families, delivery documents and targeting that matches PRC interests in Taiwan [S2][S3]; CrowdStrike, Trend Micro and FireEye reporting cited by MITRE [S4][S5][S6][S7]; Microsoft's naming map [S1].

objectives: Cyber espionage consistent with broader PRC goals, especially PRC self-interest regarding Taiwan, according to Mandiant [S2][S3]. Targeting of journalists and a major US newspaper points to intelligence collection on media coverage [S2][S3].

regions: East Asia (Ixeshe targeting since at least 2009) [S4][S7]
United States (New York Times compromise, October 2012) [S2]
targeting.notes: The August 2014 HIGHTIDE campaign targeted multiple Taiwanese government organizations between 22 and 28 August 2014. Spear-phishing emails appeared to come from valid but compromised Taiwanese government accounts [S2]. Related THREEBYTE and WATERSPOUT activity hit a Taiwanese technology company and a Japanese high-technology/electronics company, but Mandiant did not firmly attribute those two campaigns to APT12 [S2].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing with weaponized Microsoft Word and PDF attachments that exploit Office, Adobe Reader and Flash vulnerabilities, including CVE-2012-0158 [S2][S4][S6]. The group sends lures from compromised but legitimate accounts [S2][S3]. Its custom HTTP backdoors include RIPTIDE, a proxy-aware backdoor that uses RC4-encrypted C2 (also called Etumbot by Arbor); its modified successor HIGHTIDE; and THREEBYTE and WATERSPOUT, which Mandiant says are possibly related [S2][S3]. It also used the Ixeshe malware family and the HTRAN connection-proxy tool [S4][S6][S7]. Per CrowdStrike reporting cited by MITRE, the group derived C2 ports by calculating them from IP octets ('DNS calculation') and used blogs and WordPress for C2 [S4][S5]. Mandiant highlights rapid retooling after public disclosure: protocol and string changes after the June 2014 Arbor report, and TTP changes after the New York Times exposure [S2].

campaigns.name: Ixeshe operations in East Asia
campaigns.summary: Ixeshe malware is used against East Asian targets from at least 2009; MITRE associates it with APT12.

campaigns.name: IXESHE campaign (Trend Micro)
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro publishes 'IXESHE: An APT Campaign'. MITRE cites it for spear-phishing with malicious Office and PDF attachments, exploits of Office, Adobe Reader and Flash flaws, and HTRAN use.

campaigns.name: New York Times compromise
campaigns.summary: Mandiant reports that APT12 compromised the New York Times. After the intrusion was disclosed, the group paused briefly and changed its TTPs.

campaigns.name: CrowdStrike 'Whois Numbered Panda' profile
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike profiles the group as Numbered Panda. MITRE cites the profile for DNS-calculated C2 ports and blog/WordPress C2.

campaigns.name: Retooling after Arbor Etumbot disclosure
campaigns.summary: Arbor Networks publishes on the RIPTIDE (Etumbot) backdoor, which was used from 2011 to May 2014. Mandiant then sees APT12 change RIPTIDE's protocols and strings, producing HIGHTIDE.

campaigns.name: HIGHTIDE spear-phishing against Taiwan government
campaigns.summary: Between 22 and 28 August 2014, CVE-2012-0158 Word lures sent from compromised Taiwanese government accounts deliver HIGHTIDE to multiple Taiwanese government organizations. Possibly related THREEBYTE and WATERSPOUT lures target a Taiwanese technology company and a Japanese high-technology company.

diamond.adversary: PRC-based espionage operators that Mandiant believes have links to the PLA; Microsoft calls the group Hexagon Typhoon and MITRE tracks it as APT12 [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.capability: Exploit documents (CVE-2012-0158 and Adobe/Flash CVEs); RIPTIDE, HIGHTIDE, THREEBYTE, WATERSPOUT and Ixeshe backdoors; HTRAN proxying; rapid retooling after disclosure [S2][S4][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Hard-coded HTTP C2 servers, including direct IP C2 and dynamic-DNS domains for WATERSPOUT [S2]; compromised legitimate email accounts used to send lures [S2]; blogs and WordPress used for C2, with ports derived by DNS calculation [S4][S5].
diamond.victim: Taiwanese government ministries, journalists and media (New York Times), defense industrial base, and high-tech and electronics firms in Taiwan and Japan [S2][S3][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection that supports PRC strategic goals, especially regarding Taiwan, and intelligence on media coverage of China [S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Unpatched Microsoft Office and Adobe client software on Windows endpoints, plus trust in email from known colleagues [S2][S4].

gaps: No reporting on Hexagon Typhoon / APT12 activity after 2014 was found in the sources gathered. Current activity level, tooling and any re-designation are unknown.
Microsoft has published no actor profile or blog content for Hexagon Typhoon in the sources gathered; only the naming map was available [S1].

Primary documents not opened (network blocked): CrowdStrike 'Whois Numbered Panda' (2013) [S5], Trend Micro IXESHE white paper (2012) [S6], FireEye 'Survival of the Fittest' (2013) [S7], Secureworks BRONZE GLOBE profile, CFR APT12 entry, Arbor Networks Etumbot report, and Mandiant M-Trends 2014. Claims from S5 to S7 rely on MITRE ATT&CK's citations of them [S4].
Web search was unavailable for this run (shared search budget exhausted). Press coverage of the 2013 New York Times disclosure and any later reporting were not reviewed.
PLA link is a hedged vendor assessment (Mandiant). No specific PLA unit or MSS/contractor tie is public in the sources gathered, and no government attribution was found.

Alias boundary issue: MISP Galaxy's APT12 entry lists TG-2754 with the same identifier as BRONZE GLOBE [S8], but this encyclopedia maps TG-2754 to Mulberry Typhoon (APT5). This needs reconciling against Secureworks' own profiles.
THREEBYTE and WATERSPOUT campaigns were not positively attributed to APT12 by Mandiant [S2].
Aliases BeeBus, Group 22, Crimson Iron, Poisoned Flight and IXESHE-as-actor come from aggregator data (MISP) [S8], not from vendor reports reviewed here.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is user endpoints running Office and PDF readers, and the email trust relationships between government personnel, especially in Taiwan and Japan and partner organizations that work with them [S2]. STEP 2 (effects): Because email arrives from compromised colleague accounts, sender-reputation filtering is weakened. The group's quick retooling after disclosure shortens the shelf life of published signatures [S2]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Spear-phish with an exploit document from a compromised trusted account, then an HTTP backdoor (RIPTIDE/HIGHTIDE-class) with RC4-encrypted C2 or DNS-calculated ports, then document collection; HTRAN can be used to hide C2 origin [S2][S4][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued spear-phishing espionage against Taiwan-focused government, defense-industrial and media targets [S2][S3]. MDCOA is a renewed or rebranded campaign against US and partner organizations that support Taiwan, using new tooling released immediately after any public exposure [S2]. Candidate indicators: Word documents exploiting CVE-2012-0158 or newer Office flaws; executables dropped as word.exe or winword.exe in user Temp directories; HTTP beacons with anomalous User-Agent/URI patterns to direct IPs or dynamic-DNS domains; C2 ports that look computed from IP octets [S2][S4][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: public reporting on this actor stops in 2014 in the sources gathered, so treat any detection as a prompt to check current vendor reporting rather than to rely on 2014 IOCs [S2]. (2) Authorities: activity traced to commercial media or partner-nation government networks lies outside DoD defensive authorities and needs interagency and partner coordination [S2]. (3) Mission assurance: phishing from compromised partner accounts threatens DODIN users who correspond with Taiwan and Japan counterparts; prioritize patching Office and PDF readers and inspecting attachments [S2][S4]. (4) Coordination: share retooling observations quickly with partners, because Mandiant reports the actor changes tools within weeks of disclosure [S2].
